title: Never again, for anyone
hookLine: the lesson some draw: guard every people's dignity

cards: Two words. Painted on banners. Spoken at memorials.
Typed into arguments at midnight. Never again. Short enough to shout, simple enough for a child to repeat.
And the moment you say them, a question opens underneath, quietly. Never again for whom? For Jews?
For everyone? For anyone who is next? The two words themselves don't answer it.

teach.b: After the Holocaust, never again became a vow, and Jews hear it in more than one way. For some, it is first a promise that the Jewish people will never again be left defenseless, with no door open and no one coming.
For some, it is first a promise about every people: that no group anywhere will be hunted for who they are.

teach.h: FOR US, FOR EVERYONE, OR BOTH.
teach.b: And some hold both at once, and see no contradiction.
The second reading reaches back to the Torah's first page: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him." Not one nation. A human being.
The rabbis tell of a debate about the Torah's great principle. Rabbi Akiva named love your neighbor as yourself.

Ben Azzai named a verse he called greater still: the one that opens the family record of Adam, the first human, made in the likeness of God. A neighbor can be someone near; that verse takes in every human being.

And Leviticus turns the idea into a command for ordinary days: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." That's where the vow lives most of the time: not in grand moments, but in small ones.

The persecution this path has traced began small too: rights taken away, words of contempt, shops marked, doors closed. Small steps, each one easy to look away from. So the vow, in practice, is a habit.
Noticing the small step. Saying something. Not laughing.
Not standing idly by, whoever the neighbor is.

how: Jewish communities speak of never again at Holocaust memorials and in education; some Jewish groups work against antisemitism and for the protection of other peoples facing persecution.

o: a vow made after the Holocaust
a prayer of mourning said on Yom HaShoah
a peace treaty clause banning future wars

p: a principle greater than love your neighbor

s: never again is heard in only one way
some hear it for the Jewish people, some for every people, and some hold both.
in a rabbinic debate, one sage named a principle even greater than love your neighbor
Ben Azzai named the verse about the family record of Adam, made in God's likeness: it takes in every human being.
the vow lives mostly in grand historic moments
it lives in small ones: noticing, saying something, not standing idly by.

games.q: at dinner, someone makes a cruel joke about a group no one at the table belongs to. people laugh a little. what do you do?
o: say quietly that it isn't funny.
say nothing, since it isn't about you.
games.why: Leviticus says not to stand idly by while a neighbor is in danger. the vow begins in small moments like this.

practice: Think back over the past week for a moment when someone was mocked or shut out for who they are: a joke at a table, a comment online, a look on a bus.
Don't judge yourself; just find it, and calmly picture what one small act of standing up could have looked like, a word, a question, sitting beside that person afterward, until it feels possible.
If you pray, you can ask for courage.

wordCard.voice: Never again. A vow made after the Holocaust. Some hear it for the Jewish people, some for every people, and some for both.

orig.note: Hebrew, Leviticus 19:16: do not stand by your neighbor's blood.

carryVoice: Your line: whoever the neighbor is. Ben Azzai's verse leaves no one out. Until tomorrow.
